title: Corey Haines's copy-editing playbook: seven sweeps and an AI-tell check
summary: Corey's open-source copy-editing skill lays out a systematic way to improve existing marketing copy: pick an edit mode first, run seven focused sweeps (clarity, voice, so what, prove it, specificity, emotion, zero risk), then strip AI tells. It adds an expert-panel scoring gate for high-stakes copy and a content-refresh approach for decaying pages.

principles.text: Pick the edit mode first: rebuild slop from facts, restore a real voice, or make a point edit that touches only what was asked.
principles.quote: A point edit skips the Seven Sweeps: change only what was asked plus the minimum around it, return just the changed lines with a reason, and leave everything else as written.

principles.text: Edit in focused, sequential passes, looping back to earlier sweeps after each one, instead of fixing everything at once.
principles.quote: Multiple focused passes beat one unfocused review

principles.text: Run the So What test on every claim: tie each feature to a deeper benefit the reader cares about.
principles.quote: For every statement, ask "Okay, so what?" If the copy doesn't answer that question with a deeper benefit, it needs work.

principles.text: Replace vague claims with concrete numbers, timeframes and examples; if it can't be made specific, it's probably filler.
principles.quote: Remove content that can't be made specific (it's probably filler)

principles.text: Back every claim with proof such as named testimonials, data, case studies or third-party validation, or soften the claim.
Fix AI-sounding sentence shapes by rewriting from the underlying facts, not by swapping synonyms, because AI tells erode trust in nearby claims.
principles.quote: A reader who spots an AI tell tends to doubt the claims around it. The shape of a sentence gives it away more than any word does.
